references.text: The Lord has visited (פָּקַד) the children of Israel - the same expression is used for God's care for His people
The people bowed down and worshiped (וַיִּקְּדוּ וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲווּ) - an identical response to God's salvation
The Lord visited (פָּקַד) Sarah as He had said - the same verb for God's intervention
Joseph's prophecy that God would visit (פָּקַד) Israel and bring them out of Egypt
God saw (רָאָה) the affliction (עֳנִי) of the Israelites - the same word pair is used here
The people believed (וַיַּאֲמִינוּ) in the Lord - the same root for faith (אמן)
The Lord saw our affliction (עָנְיֵנוּ) - a liturgical confession that reflects this event
He looked upon them in their distress - a poetic rendering of God's care for Israel
The Lord has visited (ἐπεσκέψατο) His people - Zechariah uses the same concept regarding God's salvation
By faith (πίστει) they passed through the Red Sea - Hebrews links the people's faith to the exodus from Egypt
Both verses illustrate the theological principle that God's people turn to Him in distress and find grace through prayer and worship.
The verse describes the divine action ('God saw') which is the direct prerequisite for the people's faith and worship in Exodus 4:31.
Both verses demonstrate the theological pattern where seeing God's mighty works immediately leads to popular praise and awe.
Both verses use an identical liturgical expression to justify praise based on God's eternal mercy and goodness.
The verse shows a New Testament parallel to the Old Testament reaction where seeing God's power over suffering immediately triggers awe and praise.
